memos.scout:
The honest case for buying SARP now is weak, and I don't think it clears the bar.

What the brief shows as demand: 30 buyers and 30 sellers in the last 15 minutes, $2,120 volume, a 4.4% gain over 30 minutes, and a shallow 0.18% drawdown from the 30-minute high. Those are real trades, but they are roughly balanced (9.11 SOL bought, 8.65 SOL sold, net flow +0.46 SOL), so there's no sign of accumulating demand beyond the operator-driven launch.

The launch itself is the problem. Within two minutes of graduation, 771 SOL came from 19 buyers, the top 5 buyers account for 99.9% of early buying, and the bundle share is 100%. That is an operator-backed pattern, which has historically been roughly break-even, and the sell-to-buy ratio of 0.0003 shows almost no organic selling early on, which means the early holders haven't been tested by the market yet. The top-3 share of 1.0 means the curve is effectively controlled by a few wallets, who can exit at any time.

Against a 1.4-5.1% round-trip cost, a break-even base rate gives no edge. I'd skip this coin. There is no strong case that demand will persist 30-60 minutes out.

The curve data reinforces this: bundle_share and top3_share are both 1.0, and the completer_share of 2.87 suggests the operator is positioned to exit. Recent flow is already tilting toward sellers. In the last 15 minutes, sell_sol (8.65) nearly matched buy_sol (9.11), with the same 30 sellers as buyers and a net flow of only 0.46 SOL. The sell-to-buy ratio of 0.0003 at launch is not a bullish sign either, since it reflects how little real two-sided trading occurred. Round-trip costs of 1.4-5.1% on a $20 ticket would be eaten by even a modest distribution, and a 0.18% drawdown from the high tells us nothing about whether the operator is done selling. Skip.
